original_question: For a graph G and a graph property P, let beta_P(G) be the maximum size of a matching M whose induced subgraph <M> has property P. For the P-matching parameters introduced in the survey, what is the computational complexity of determining beta_P(G), and for which graph classes can beta_P(G) be computed in polynomial time or shown NP-complete?
target_in_paper: The draft is closest to the survey’s algorithmic open problems for maximum P-matchings: determine the computational complexity of the disconnected matching number β_dc(G), and find fast polynomial-time algorithms for the acyclic matching number β_ac(G) on special graph classes, explicitly including interval graphs.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly uses the P-matching viewpoint, correctly treats β_P(G) as a maximum-cardinality parameter, and correctly focuses on computational complexity and tractable graph classes. It also aligns with the survey’s emphasis on induced-subgraph restrictions on matchings rather than ordinary maximum matching.
missing_details: The paper does not pose a single broad open problem asking for a full complexity classification of all β_P parameters; that broadening goes beyond the survey’s actual intent.

The survey’s unresolved maximum-parameter questions are narrower: the complexity of the disconnected matching number β_dc(G), and fast algorithms for the acyclic matching number β_ac(G) on special graph classes.
You should specify that G[M] denotes the subgraph induced by the vertices saturated by the matching M.
You should name the relevant properties P from the survey’s seven examples: ordinary, induced, uniquely restricted, connected, isolatefree, acyclic, and disconnected.

The paper already records that connected and isolatefree matching numbers are polynomial-time computable, while induced, uniquely restricted, and acyclic matching are already hard in general; so asking for the complexity of all β_P is broader than the paper.
If graph classes are mentioned in the refined question, the paper-faithful example is interval graphs for β_ac, rather than an unrestricted request for all graph classes.
Your draft should avoid drifting into the lower parameters (minimum cardinality of maximal P-matchings), which are separate problems in the literature and not what your current wording targets.
refined_question: For a graph G and a matching M, let G[M] be the subgraph induced by the vertices saturated by M. The survey considers the seven maximum P-matching parameters β_P(G) obtained when P is, respectively, the properties of being an arbitrary graph, 1-regular (induced), having a unique perfect matching (uniquely restricted), connected, isolatefree, acyclic, or disconnected. Complete the remaining algorithmic picture left open there by determining the computational complexity of the disconnected matching number β_dc(G), and by identifying special graph classes—explicitly including interval graphs—on which the acyclic matching number β_ac(G) can be computed in polynomial time.
justification: The paper is a brief survey rather than a new full classification theorem. The foundational P-matching framework introduces seven specific maximum parameters, and the standard NP-hardness transfer theorem shows that hardness is typical for many induced-hereditary properties. Within that framework, the algorithmic discussion isolates two maximum-parameter questions that remain genuinely open at the level your draft is aiming at: the complexity of β_dc(G), and fast algorithms for β_ac(G) on special classes such as interval graphs. So the draft is directionally right but too broad: it asks for a global complexity taxonomy for all β_P and all graph classes, whereas the survey’s actual intent is much narrower and centered on those two residual questions.
